The Pine siskin (Spinus pinus) is a small, highly nomadic finch of the family Fringillidae, widely distributed across North America. Upon emergence from the shell, nestlings exhibit a relatively modest mass; data from captive-reared broods indicate that the wet weight at birth averages approximately 1.1 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.1 grams], a value consistent with the altricial development strategy typical of cardueline finches. This initial mass is sustained by frequent parental provisioning during the first days post-hatching. The developmental trajectory of the nestling proceeds rapidly thereafter, with individuals attaining a peak adult body mass of 12.7 grams [Wwi = 12.7 grams] by the time they leave the nest, reflecting the species' high metabolic demands during the short, intensive growth phase characteristic of boreal-breeding passerines. Eggs incubated under controlled laboratory conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] yield a mean incubation period of 13 days [ab = 13 days] before hatching commences, a duration that aligns closely with estimates for other North American congeneric carduelids of comparable egg size. The incubation process itself, largely performed by the female, involves tight thermal regulation of the developing embryo to maintain this targeted temperature, which is likely near optimal for rapid organogenesis within the calcareous egg.

The reproductive schedule of the Pine siskin is characterized by a moderate annual output, dictated by the brief window of food abundance in northern coniferous forests. Females typically produce between 1 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 5 eggs per clutch], with clutch size exhibiting considerable variation linked to local resource availability and female body condition at the onset of laying. Larger clutches are generally associated with years of high seed crops from spruce and pine trees. Furthermore, under favorable foraging conditions, a pair may initiate approximately 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches per year], though this figure is an average and often falls to a single successful brood in poor food years. The combination of a moderate clutch size and the capacity for a second nesting attempt yields a maximum reproductive rate that allows populations to capitalize opportunistically on mast events, a critical life-history adaptation for an irruptive species. The timing of the first breeding event in an individual's life is also tightly linked to the availability of this high-energy seed diet, which is necessary to support the substantial metabolic costs of egg production and incubation.

The initial phase of growth, from the fertilised ovum through the incubation period, begins with a very modest starting mass. The freshly laid egg, prior to any substantive embryonic development, has an initial wet weight of approximately 1.39 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.39 grams], reflecting the relatively small investment per offspring typical of a species that produces multiple-egg clutches. This value, measured gravimetrically from freshly collected clutches, represents the baseline from which embryonic growth proceeds, fueled entirely by the yolk reserves encased within the calcareous shell. Following the completion of the 13-day incubation period at 36 °C, the resulting hatchling emerges at a wet weight of about 1.1 grams [Wwb = about 1.1 grams], indicating that a significant proportion of the initial egg mass is converted into embryonic tissue and absorbed during development. The difference between the initial egg mass and the birth mass largely represents the metabolic cost of embryogenesis, including the heat production necessary to sustain development at the incubation temperature, as well as the water loss that occurs through the porous eggshell over the incubation period.

Longevity records for the Pine siskin, compiled from mark-recapture studies and banding returns, indicate that this species possesses a modest lifespan relative to many other passerines of similar body size. Under optimal thermal conditions at approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the oldest documented individual recovered in the wild reached an age of 11 years [am = 11 years], a record that underscores the species' potential for extended survival under favorable conditions, particularly in years of sustained food availability. This lifespan, when considered in the context of the species' high annual reproductive output and irruptive migration patterns, suggests a life-history strategy that balances moderate adult survival with the capacity for rapid population increase during boom periods. At the core of this strategy lies the maximum reproductive rate, expressed as the product of clutch size and frequency. The first successful brood is typically initiated at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning most individuals delay their first reproduction until the spring following their birth year, a pattern common among temperate-zone passerines that allows for complete somatic development and the establishment of a winter fat reserve before the energetic demands of breeding commence at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].
